curriculum_source: CFA Program 2027 Level III, Volume 3 (Performance Measurement), Learning Module 2: Investment Manager Selection

drills.los_text: describe the components of a manager selection process, including due diligence

questions.stem: Investment manager due diligence is best described as:

options.A: a legal review of a manager's regulatory registration.
options.B: a quantitative screen ranking managers' historical returns.
options.C: investigation and analysis supporting an investment decision.

rationales.A: This narrows due diligence to a compliance check. Due diligence is the investigation and analysis in support of an investment action, decision, or recommendation, and it spans the investment process, the firm's integrity, its operations, and its personnel. Confirming registration and compliance status is one small input to the operational side of that work, not a description of the whole exercise.
rationales.B: Due diligence involves both quantitative and qualitative analysis, and its focus is on understanding how the investment results were achieved — not on ranking a track record. A returns-only screen says nothing about whether the process that generated those returns is repeatable, whether the people who ran it are still there, or whether the firm's operations can be relied upon.
rationales.C: Due diligence is the investigation and analysis in support of an investment action, decision, or recommendation. In manager due diligence the focus is on understanding how the investment results were achieved and on assessing the likelihood that the investment process which generated those returns will produce superior, or at least satisfactory, results going forward. It also entails an evaluation of the firm's integrity, operations, and personnel. Because both the repeatability of the process and the soundness of the firm are at issue, due diligence necessarily involves quantitative analysis of the record and qualitative analysis of the process behind it.

questions.stem: The three broad components of manager search and selection are most likely:

options.A: philosophy, process, and people.
options.B: the universe, quantitative analysis, and qualitative analysis.
options.C: screening, interviewing, and contract negotiation.

rationales.A: Philosophy, process and people (together with portfolio) are the key aspects of investment due diligence, which sits inside the qualitative component. They are not the three broad components of the search itself, which are the universe, a quantitative analysis of the manager's performance track record, and a qualitative analysis of the manager's investment process.
rationales.B: The manager search and selection process has three broad components: (1) the universe — defining the feasible set of managers, considering suitability, style, and active versus passive; (2) a quantitative analysis of the manager's performance track record, including attribution and appraisal measures, capture ratios, and drawdown; and (3) a qualitative analysis of the manager's investment process. The qualitative component itself consists of investment due diligence, which evaluates the manager's investment process, and operational due diligence, which evaluates the manager's infrastructure and firm.
rationales.C: This invents a procedural list of search activities. Screening, interviewing and negotiating terms are tasks performed along the way; the three broad components of the process are the universe, the quantitative analysis of the track record, and the qualitative analysis of the investment process and the firm.

questions.stem: Qualitative analysis of manager selection most likely consists of:

options.A: historical returns and performance attribution statistics.
options.B: investment due diligence and operational due diligence.
options.C: the same work as quantitative analysis, under another label.

rationales.A: Returns and attribution statistics are the quantitative component of manager selection — the analysis of the performance track record, including appraisal measures, capture ratios and drawdown. The qualitative side is investment due diligence, which evaluates philosophy, process, people and portfolio, plus operational due diligence, which evaluates the firm and its infrastructure.
rationales.B: The qualitative analysis consists of investment due diligence, which evaluates the manager's investment process, and operational due diligence, which evaluates the manager's infrastructure and firm. Investment due diligence asks which manager best fits the portfolio need and whether the manager can be expected to keep generating that return distribution; its key aspects are philosophy, process, people and portfolio. Operational due diligence asks whether the track record is accurate and fully reflects the risks taken; its key aspects are process and procedure, the firm, the investment vehicle, the terms, and ongoing monitoring.
rationales.C: The two components are distinct and answer different questions. Quantitative analysis evaluates the return record — what was achieved and with what risk. Qualitative analysis evaluates how it was achieved and whether the arrangement can be relied upon, through investment due diligence on the process and operational due diligence on the firm and its infrastructure. Neither substitutes for the other.

questions.stem: Operational due diligence of an investment manager most likely evaluates:

options.A: philosophy and people.
options.B: back-office process and procedure.
options.C: philosophy, process, people, and portfolio.

rationales.A: Philosophy and people are key aspects of investment due diligence, which evaluates the manager's investment process: philosophy asks what market inefficiency the manager seeks to exploit, and people asks whether the investment personnel have the expertise and experience to implement the process. Process and procedures, by contrast, are key aspects of operational due diligence.
rationales.B: Operational due diligence evaluates the manager's infrastructure and firm. Its key aspects are: process and procedure — is the back office strong, safeguarding assets and able to issue accurate reports in a timely manner; the firm — is it profitable, with a healthy culture, likely to remain in business, and committed to delivering performance rather than gathering assets; the investment vehicle — is it suitable for the portfolio need; the terms — are they acceptable and appropriate for the strategy and the vehicle; and monitoring — does the manager continue to be the best fit for the portfolio need. Process and procedures are operational-due-diligence aspects, whereas people and philosophy belong to investment due diligence.
rationales.C: Philosophy, process, people and portfolio are the four key aspects of investment due diligence — the manager's investment approach and its implementation. Operational due diligence covers a different list: process and procedure, the firm, the investment vehicle, the terms, and monitoring.

questions.stem: Investment due diligence of an investment manager most likely evaluates:

options.A: the investment vehicle and its terms.
options.B: back-office process and procedure.
options.C: the manager's investment philosophy.

rationales.A: The investment vehicle and the terms are evaluated under operational due diligence, which asks whether the vehicle is suitable for the portfolio need and whether the terms are acceptable and appropriate for the strategy and the vehicle. Investment due diligence has four aspects instead: philosophy, process, people and portfolio.
rationales.B: Back-office process and procedure — whether the back office is strong, safeguards assets, and can issue accurate reports in a timely manner — is a key aspect of operational due diligence. Investment due diligence evaluates philosophy, the investment process itself, people, and portfolio construction.
rationales.C: Investment due diligence evaluates: philosophy — what market inefficiency does the manager seek to exploit; process — is the investment process capable of exploiting that inefficiency; people — do the investment personnel possess the expertise and experience necessary to implement the process effectively; and portfolio — is portfolio construction consistent with the stated investment philosophy and process. Philosophy is the first of those four aspects, so it falls squarely within investment due diligence, while the vehicle, the terms and the back office belong to operational due diligence.

questions.stem: An underlying assumption of investment manager due diligence is most likely that:

options.A: past outperformance mechanically repeats.
options.B: a consistent process produces a similar return distribution relative to risk factors.
options.C: manager returns are random.

rationales.A: The assumption concerns the consistency of the process, not naive persistence of past returns. What is assumed is that a consistent, robust investment process will generate a similar return distribution relative to risk factors through time, provided the underlying dynamics of the market have not changed dramatically. A manager whose past outperformance came from sources the process cannot repeat fails that test, which is exactly why due diligence examines the process rather than extrapolating the record.
rationales.B: An underlying assumption of investment manager due diligence is that a consistent, robust investment process will generate a similar return distribution relative to risk factors through time, assuming the underlying dynamics of the market have not dramatically changed. One important goal of manager due diligence is therefore to understand whether the manager's investment process, people, and portfolio construction satisfy that assumption — that is, whether the investment process will generate the expected return from the expected sources.
rationales.C: The premise is the opposite. If returns were random there would be nothing to evaluate and no basis for selecting one manager over another. Due diligence proceeds on the view that a robust, consistent process produces behavior that is evaluable and repeatable relative to risk factors, which is what makes examining the process, the people and the portfolio construction worthwhile.

questions.stem: The manager search and selection process most likely begins by:

options.A: including every available manager in the search.
options.B: defining the universe of feasible managers.
options.C: selecting the single best-performing manager.

rationales.A: The objective is to reduce the manager universe to a manageable size relative to the resources and time available to evaluate it, which means balancing the risk of too narrow a search, which potentially excludes interesting managers, against the risk of too broad a search, which yields little gain in reducing the list of potential managers. Including every available manager maximizes the second of those risks and leaves the search no more informative.
rationales.B: The manager selection process begins by defining the universe of feasible managers — those managers that potentially satisfy the identified portfolio need. The objective is to reduce the manager universe to a manageable size relative to the resources and time available to evaluate it, and this involves balancing the risks of too narrow a search, which potentially excludes interesting managers, and too broad a search, which leads to little gain in reducing the list of potential managers. The IPS and the reason for the manager search largely determine the universe of managers considered and the benchmark against which they are compared.
rationales.C: This reverses the process. A feasible universe is defined first, from the portfolio need and the IPS, and then reduced to a manageable size; candidates are compared within that universe and against the relevant benchmark. Starting from a top performer and working outward lets one manager's past record define the feasible set, rather than the portfolio need.

questions.stem: A manager search undertaken to add a new strategic or tactical exposure most likely examines:

options.A: only the managers covered by the consultant's database.
options.B: a broad universe of comparable managers.
options.C: the identical universe examined in every other search.

rationales.A: The purpose of the search, not the convenience of a particular database, determines how wide the net is cast. A new search based on a strategic or tactical view examines a broad universe of comparable managers and looks to select the best within that universe; the IPS and the reason for the search largely determine the universe considered and the benchmark against which candidates are compared. Database coverage is a practical constraint to work around, not the definition of the feasible set.
rationales.B: A new search based on a strategic or tactical view, such as adding a new strategy or risk exposure, will examine a broad universe of comparable managers and look to select the best within the universe. By contrast, adding a manager to increase capacity or diversification within a strategy already held will look for a complement to current holdings, and replacing a single manager in a particular strategy will look for the best manager within that strategy universe. The IPS in part determines what the relative terms best, complement, and cost/benefit mean in each case.
rationales.C: Scope varies with purpose. Adding a new strategic or tactical exposure calls for a broad scan of comparable managers to find the best within the universe; adding capacity or diversification within a strategy already held is narrower and profile-driven, since the aim is a complement to current holdings; replacing a manager is narrower still, confined to that strategy's universe.

drills.los_text: contrast Type I and Type II errors in manager hiring and continuation decisions

questions.stem: A Type I error in manager selection is most likely:

options.A: hiring a manager who subsequently underperforms expectations.
options.B: failing to reject a false null of no skill.
options.C: not hiring a manager who subsequently outperforms.

rationales.A: A Type I error is a false positive: the null hypothesis of no skill is rejected when that null is in fact correct. Operationally, it is hiring or retaining a manager who subsequently underperforms expectations. The decision to act was taken on evidence of skill that was not there.
rationales.B: Failing to reject the null of no skill when the null is actually false is a Type II error, a false negative. A Type I error is the mirror image: rejecting a null that is correct, which is why it is described as a false positive.
rationales.C: Not hiring, or firing, a manager who subsequently outperforms is the Type II error, a false negative. This option attaches the false-negative definition to the Type I label and so confuses the two error types.

questions.stem: A Type II error in manager selection is most likely:

options.A: rejecting a null of no skill that is actually true.
options.B: hiring a manager who subsequently underperforms.
options.C: not hiring a manager who subsequently outperforms.

rationales.A: Rejecting the null hypothesis of no skill when that null is correct is a Type I error, a false positive. A Type II error runs the other way: the null is not rejected even though it is incorrect.
rationales.B: Hiring or retaining a manager who subsequently underperforms expectations is the Type I error, a false positive. This option states the false-positive definition under the Type II label and so confuses the two error types.
rationales.C: A Type II error is a false negative: the null hypothesis of no skill is not rejected when that null is incorrect. Operationally, it is not hiring, or firing, a manager who subsequently outperforms, or performs in line with, expectations. The skill was present but the evidence was judged insufficient to act on.

questions.stem: In the manager selection process, hypothesis testing most likely:

options.A: begins from a null hypothesis of no manager skill.
options.B: begins from a null hypothesis of demonstrated skill.
options.C: has no role, as skill cannot be framed statistically.

rationales.A: The determination of whether a manager is skillful typically starts with the null hypothesis, the hypothesis assumed to be true until demonstrated otherwise, that the manager is not skillful. The two ways that test can fail follow directly from it: rejecting this null when it is correct is a Type I error, and not rejecting this null when it is incorrect is a Type II error.
rationales.B: The null is that the manager is not skillful, and evidence has to overturn it. Starting instead from an assumed presence of skill reverses the burden of proof: the manager is hired and retained unless performance disproves a skill that was never demonstrated, which is precisely the route to Type I errors.
rationales.C: Manager selection is framed explicitly as a hypothesis test built on the no-skill null, with Type I and Type II errors as the two ways the test can go wrong. Skill is treated as a statistical proposition about the manager's return distribution, not as something outside the reach of testing.

questions.stem: The relative attention decision makers give to Type I and Type II errors in manager selection is most likely explained by:

options.A: greater concern with Type II errors, as missed opportunities are painful.
options.B: greater concern with Type I errors, as mistaken rejections cause regret.
options.C: equal concern with both, as the two errors cost the same.

rationales.A: Attention runs the other way: decision makers appear predisposed to worry more about Type I errors. Type I errors are errors of commission, a mistaken hire or retention, and they generate regret and an explicit cost; the opportunities missed through Type II errors usually pass unnoticed, so they attract less attention rather than more.
rationales.B: Decision makers appear predisposed to worry more about Type I errors than Type II errors, for several reasons. Psychologically, people seek to avoid feelings of regret, and Type I errors are mistaken rejections whereas Type II errors are failures to detect a true relationship. As a result, Type I errors create explicit costs while Type II errors create only opportunity costs, and because individuals put less weight on opportunity costs, Type I errors are psychologically the more painful. Type I errors are also relatively straightforward to measure and are often linked directly to the decision maker's compensation. They are more transparent to investors as well, so they entail not only the regret of an incorrect decision but the pain of having to explain that decision to the investor. Type II errors are far less transparent unless the investor tracks the managers who were not hired or were fired.
rationales.C: The attention given to the two error types is asymmetric, not equal, and the reasons are psychological as much as economic. Type I errors carry explicit costs, are straightforward to measure, are often tied to the decision maker's compensation and are visible to investors; Type II errors register only as opportunity costs, which individuals weight less heavily.

questions.stem: The cost of a Type I or Type II error in manager selection most likely:

options.A: varies with the return distributions of the skilled and unskilled managers in the universe.
options.B: varies only with the fee differential between active and passive options.
options.C: is fixed, whatever the composition of the manager universe.

rationales.A: The cost is driven by the size, shape, mean and dispersion of the return distributions of the skilled and unskilled managers within the universe. The smaller the difference in sample size and in distribution mean, and the wider the dispersion of the distributions, the smaller the expected cost of a Type I or Type II error, because the two populations are harder to tell apart and less is forgone by misclassifying one. More efficient markets are likely to exhibit smaller differences between the distributions of skilled and unskilled managers, which indicates a lower opportunity cost of retaining an unskilled manager and a lower cost of hiring one.
rationales.B: Fees matter to net return, but the cost of these errors is driven by the return distributions of skilled versus unskilled managers: their size, shape, mean and dispersion. A fee differential says nothing about how distinguishable the two populations are, which is what determines how much a misclassification forgoes.
rationales.C: The costs are not constants. They vary with the composition of the manager universe, because it is the distributions of skilled and unskilled manager returns that determine what is forgone by rejecting a skilled manager or incurred by retaining an unskilled one. Where those distributions overlap closely, as in more efficient markets, both error costs are smaller.

questions.stem: The monitoring of managers in a selection process most likely:

options.A: serves no purpose once a manager is rejected.
options.B: reveals weaknesses through patterns of Type II error.
options.C: covers only the managers currently held in the portfolio.

rationales.A: Monitoring the managers who were not hired and those who were fired is what reveals patterns of Type II error and behavioural bias in the selection process. Rejected managers therefore remain informative: their subsequent performance is the only evidence of the decisions the process got wrong by omission.
rationales.B: Although Type I errors are more familiar and more of a concern to most decision makers, a consistent pattern of Type II errors can highlight weaknesses in the manager selection process. The approach is to monitor not only the managers currently held but also those evaluated and not hired and those who were fired. The goal is to determine whether there are identifiable factors that differentiate managers hired from managers not hired, whether those factors are consistent with the decision maker's investment philosophy and process, what factors drive the decision to retain or fire a manager, and what value the decisions to retain or fire actually added. The objective is to avoid decisions based on short-term performance, that is, trend following, and to identify any evidence of behavioural biases such as regret and loss aversion in the evaluation of managers during selection.
rationales.C: The approach deliberately extends beyond current holdings to the managers evaluated but not hired and the managers who were fired. Restricting monitoring to retained managers leaves Type II errors invisible, since a skilled manager passed over or dismissed never appears in the portfolio's own record.

questions.stem: The cost of a Type I error in manager selection is most likely:

options.A: failing to hire a manager who had genuine skill.
options.B: no different from the cost of a Type II error.
options.C: holding a manager without skill.

rationales.A: Failing to hire a skilled manager is the cost of a Type II error, not a Type I error. The Type I cost is the opposite: retaining or hiring a manager who has no skill.
rationales.B: The two costs differ, and both are driven by the size, shape, mean and dispersion of the skilled and unskilled return distributions. A Type I error incurs the cost of holding an unskilled manager; a Type II error forgoes the return of a skilled one, which is an opportunity cost rather than an explicit one.
rationales.C: The cost of a Type I error is holding a manager without skill, as against the cost of a Type II error, which is not holding managers with skill. The magnitudes depend on how distinguishable the two populations are: the less distinct the distribution of skilled managers from that of unskilled managers, the lower both the opportunity cost of retaining and the cost of hiring an unskilled manager, so the smaller the perceived difference between the two distributions, the lower the cost of, and the incentive for, firing a manager. The amounts at stake are large. Individual investors significantly underperform the average mutual fund because of poor timing and fund selection decisions, and a study of institutional plan sponsor allocation decisions found that investment products receiving contributions subsequently underperformed products experiencing withdrawals, with more than $170 billion estimated to have been lost over the period examined (Stewart, Neumann, Knittel, and Heisler 2009).

drills.los_text: describe uses of returns-based and holdings-based style analysis in investment manager selection

questions.stem: Style analysis in the manager selection process most likely:

options.A: is an important component of performance appraisal.
options.B: relies solely on the manager's self-reported classification.
options.C: is used mainly to set the manager's advisory fee.

rationales.A: An important component of performance appraisal and manager selection is understanding a manager's risk exposures relative to the benchmark and how those exposures evolve over time; that process is style analysis. The understanding it gives helps define the universe of potential managers and supports the monitoring of the managers selected. A manager's self-reported risk exposures, such as portfolio concentration, industry exposure, capitalisation exposure and other quantitative measures, are the starting point: they allow managers to be classified by style for the selection process, give a reference point for evaluating returns-based and holdings-based style analysis, and serve as an operational check on the manager. The results of returns-based style analysis and holdings-based style analysis should be consistent with the manager's stated philosophy and investment process; if they are not, the process might not be repeatable or might be implemented inconsistently.
rationales.B: Self-reported exposures are only the starting point of style analysis. Returns-based and holdings-based style analyses verify them independently, and any inconsistency between the two and the manager's stated philosophy is itself a finding about whether the process is repeatable.
rationales.C: Style analysis exists to establish a manager's risk exposures relative to the benchmark and how they evolve, which is what defines the universe of candidate managers and drives the monitoring of those selected. Fee setting is not its purpose.

questions.stem: A requirement for style analysis to be useful is most likely that it be:

options.A: meaningful.
options.B: low cost.
options.C: audited.

rationales.A: Returns-based and holdings-based style analyses provide a means of determining the risks and the sources of return for a particular strategy. To be useful, style analysis must be meaningful, in that the risks reported represent the important sources of performance return and risk; accurate, in that the reported values reflect the manager's actual risk exposures; consistent, in that the methodology allows comparison over time and across multiple managers; and timely, in that the report is available soon enough to be useful in making informed investment decisions.
rationales.B: Cost is not one of the stated requirements. To be useful, style analysis must be meaningful, accurate, consistent and timely; an inexpensive analysis that misstates the manager's exposures or arrives too late to act on fails every one of those tests.
rationales.C: Independent audit is not among the requirements. Accuracy is, and it means that the reported values reflect the manager's actual risk exposures, which returns-based analysis supports by using return data that are not subject to window dressing. The four requirements are that the analysis be meaningful, accurate, consistent and timely.

questions.stem: Returns-based style analysis (RBSA) is most likely an approach that:

options.A: estimates portfolio sensitivities to market indexes.
options.B: classifies style by examining each portfolio holding individually.
options.C: relies on interviews about the manager's stated philosophy.

rationales.A: Returns-based style analysis is a top-down approach that involves estimating a portfolio's sensitivities to security market indexes representing a range of distinct factors. Although it adds the analytical step of estimating the risk factors, rather than taking a third-party or self-reported style categorisation at face value, the analysis is straightforward and typically does not require a large amount of additional or hard-to-acquire data. It should identify the important drivers of return and the risk factors for the period analysed, and it can be estimated even for complicated strategies. The process is also comparable across managers and through time, the use of return data provides an objective style check that is not subject to window dressing, and it can be run as soon as the return data are available.
rationales.B: Examining holdings one by one is holdings-based style analysis. Returns-based style analysis works top down from the return series, regressing portfolio returns on indexes that represent distinct style factors, which is why it can be applied to complicated strategies and to managers who will not disclose positions.
rationales.C: Returns-based style analysis is quantitative: it estimates the portfolio's return sensitivities to market indexes representing distinct factors. A manager's stated philosophy is the self-reported starting point that the analysis is meant to test, and the value of using return data is precisely that it is objective and not subject to window dressing.

questions.stem: Returns-based style analysis (RBSA) is most likely subject to:

options.A: a requirement for full position-level transparency from the manager.
options.B: imprecision from averaging exposures over the period.
options.C: no meaningful disadvantage.

rationales.A: Needing only a return series, rather than position-level holdings, is RBSA's advantage, not its drawback: it can be run on any manager who reports returns, including one unwilling or unable to disclose positions. The real disadvantage is imprecision, because the regression attributes performance to a single unchanging average portfolio over the estimation window.
rationales.B: RBSA is an imprecise tool. The additional computational effort required is not onerous, but accuracy may be compromised because RBSA effectively attributes performance to an unchanging average portfolio during the period. That averaging limits the ability to identify the impact of dynamic investment decisions and may distort the decomposition across sources of added value. The portfolio being analyzed might also not reflect current or future portfolio exposures. If the portfolio contains illiquid securities, stale prices may understate the risk exposure of the strategy, which is a particular problem for private equity (PE) and venture capital (VC) managers holding illiquid or non-traded securities; those firms report performance based on the internal rate of return of cash distributions and appraisals of ongoing projects, so reported performance can understate return volatility over shorter horizons or periods with limited liquidity events.
rationales.C: Imprecision and the averaging of exposures are real limitations, so RBSA is not free of disadvantages. Nor has it displaced holdings-based analysis: the two are complements rather than substitutes, with RBSA run from a return series alone and holdings-based analysis run from the actual positions at a point in time.

questions.stem: Holdings-based style analysis (HBSA) is most likely described as:

options.A: a top-down regression of portfolio returns on style-factor indexes.
options.B: an average of style exposures estimated over a multi-period return history.
options.C: a bottom-up estimate of risk exposures from the securities actually held.

rationales.A: That describes returns-based style analysis (RBSA), which regresses the manager's return series on a set of style-factor indexes and never looks at an individual position. HBSA works in the opposite direction, bottom-up from the actual securities in the portfolio.
rationales.B: HBSA captures a point-in-time snapshot of the holdings currently in the portfolio. Estimating an average exposure across a multi-period return history is RBSA's method, and the averaging it entails is RBSA's weakness rather than HBSA's.
rationales.C: Holdings-based style analysis is a bottom-up approach that estimates the risk exposures from the actual securities held in the portfolio at a point in time. This approach allows for estimation of current risk factors and offers several advantages. Similar to RBSA, HBSA should identify all the important drivers of return and the risk factors; be comparable across managers and through time; provide an accurate view of the manager's risk exposures, although potentially subject to window dressing; and be capable of being estimated immediately after the data become available.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of holdings-based style analysis (HBSA) is most likely:

options.A: computational effort that rises with strategy complexity and depends on manager transparency.
options.B: an inability to detect style drift, its only weakness.
options.C: no disadvantage at all.

rationales.A: The computational effort increases with the complexity of the strategy and depends on the timing and degree of the transparency provided by the manager. That extra effort can be challenging for hedge fund, private equity, and venture capital managers that may be averse to or unable to provide position-level pricing, and even with mutual funds the necessary transparency may come with a time lag. The usefulness of the analysis may also be compromised because the portfolio reflects a snapshot in time and might not reflect the portfolio going forward, particularly for high-turnover strategies. Some factors may be difficult to estimate if the strategy is complex, because HBSA requires an understanding of the underlying strategy. In general, HBSA is typically easier with equity strategies, particularly for ETFs, because holdings are published daily. If the portfolio has illiquid securities, stale pricing may underestimate the risk exposure of the strategy.
rationales.B: Style drift is exactly what a holdings snapshot reveals, since the current positions are observed directly rather than inferred from a return regression. HBSA's weaknesses lie elsewhere: computational effort, the time lag in position data, and dependence on the manager's willingness and ability to disclose positions.
rationales.C: Using actual positions does not make the approach free of drawbacks. The computational burden grows with the complexity of the strategy, and the results depend on the timing and degree of manager transparency. A snapshot can also go stale for a high-turnover portfolio, and illiquid holdings carried at stale prices underestimate the strategy's risk exposure.

questions.stem: Tracking the results of returns-based and holdings-based style analysis over time is most likely intended to:

options.A: screen a manager once, at the point of initial hire.
options.B: recompute management fees against style-adjusted benchmarks.
options.C: detect exposures drifting from the manager's stated style.

rationales.A: Style analysis is a monitoring tool, not a one-time screen. Tracking it through time is what reveals whether a manager's risk trends and exposures are moving away from the mandate after hire, which a single pre-hire snapshot cannot show.
rationales.B: Fee computation is not the purpose. The results are tracked to monitor risk trends and the development of style drift, not to recalculate compensation.
rationales.C: The results of the returns-based style analysis and the holdings-based style analysis should be tracked over time in order to ascertain whether the risk trends or exposures are out of line with expectations or with the manager's stated style; deviations may signal that issues such as style drift are developing. Style analysis is most useful with strategies that hold publicly traded securities, where pricing is frequent. It can be applied to other strategies, such as hedge funds and private equity, but the insights drawn from a style analysis of such strategies are more likely to be used for designing additional lines of inquiry in the course of due diligence than for confirmation of the investment process.

drills.los_text: describe uses of the upside capture ratio, downside capture ratio, maximum drawdown, drawdown duration, and up/down capture in evaluating managers

questions.stem: The reason drawdowns and capture ratios matter in manager evaluation is most likely that:

options.A: small losses and equal-sized gains offset one another symmetrically.
options.B: large losses require proportionally greater gains to offset.
options.C: drawdowns concern only investors early in their horizon.

rationales.A: Recovery is asymmetric rather than symmetric: a loss and a gain of the same percentage do not cancel, because the gain is earned on the smaller base left after the loss. That asymmetry is precisely why drawdowns and capture ratios matter in evaluating a manager.
rationales.B: Because large losses require proportionally greater gains to reverse or offset them, drawdowns and capture ratios can be important factors in investment manager evaluation. A manager that experiences larger drawdowns may be less suitable for an investor closer to the end of their investment horizon, who has less time for the recovery to occur. The capture ratio helps assess manager suitability relative to the investor's IPS, especially in relation to the investor's time horizon and risk tolerance.
rationales.C: The concern runs the other way. Larger drawdowns weigh most on an investor closer to the end of the investment horizon, who has little time left for the compensating gains to arrive; an investor early in a long horizon can absorb a deep drawdown and still recover.

questions.stem: Regarding upside capture (UC), downside capture (DC), and the capture ratio (CR), the most likely accurate statement is that:

options.A: the capture ratio is upside capture divided by downside capture.
options.B: the capture ratio is downside capture divided by upside capture.
options.C: upside capture is measured when the manager's own return is positive.

rationales.A: Upside capture measures capture when the benchmark return is positive, and a UC greater than 100% suggests outperformance relative to the benchmark. Downside capture measures capture when the benchmark return is negative, and a DC less than 100% generally suggests outperformance relative to the benchmark. The capture ratio is upside capture divided by downside capture, and it measures the asymmetry of return. A related measure, drawdown, is the cumulative peak-to-trough loss during a particular continuous period, and drawdown duration is the total time from the start of the drawdown until the cumulative drawdown recovers to zero.
rationales.B: The ratio is inverted here. The capture ratio is upside capture divided by downside capture, so a higher ratio indicates more favorable asymmetry: more of the benchmark's gains kept per unit of participation in its losses.
rationales.C: Both capture statistics are defined over periods classified by the sign of the benchmark return, not by the sign of the manager's own return. Upside capture is the manager's participation in the periods when the benchmark was up, and downside capture the participation in the periods when it was down.

questions.stem: A long-only strategy that holds the benchmark index in full in every month, up or down, most likely has upside capture, downside capture, and a capture ratio, respectively, closest to:

rationales.A: These are the figures for a low-beta profile, which holds half its assets in the index and the remainder in 90-day Treasury bills in every month. It captures about half of each benchmark move in both directions, so its captures are 50% and 50% and its capture ratio is still 1.0, but its participation is only half of the fully invested case.
rationales.B: A strategy allocated 100% to the index throughout the period captures the benchmark's return in full in up months and in full in down months, so upside capture is 100%, downside capture is 100%, and the capture ratio, upside capture divided by downside capture, is 1.0. That is a symmetric return profile: it neither adds convexity nor cushions losses. It contrasts with a positive asymmetry profile, allocated 75% to the index in up months and 25% in down months, giving UC 75%, DC 25%, and a ratio of 3.0; a low-beta profile, allocated 50% throughout, giving UC 50%, DC 50%, and a ratio of 1.0; and a negative asymmetry profile, allocated 25% in up months and 75% in down months, giving UC 25%, DC 75%, and a ratio of 0.3. Figures of this kind are computed from realized monthly returns over a long window, for instance January 2000 through December 2013, a period that encompasses two significant drawdowns: the bursting of the tech bubble in the early 2000s and the extreme drawdown of the global financial crisis in 2008 and 2009.
rationales.C: These are the figures for a convex, positively asymmetric strategy that holds 75% of the index in up months and 25% in down months, so it keeps three-quarters of the gains and takes a quarter of the losses. A long-only strategy that is always fully invested tracks the benchmark in both directions, so its two captures are equal rather than three times apart.

questions.stem: A strategy that is designed to produce a positively asymmetric, convex return profile relative to an equity index most likely allocates to the index:

options.A: 25% in up months and 75% in down months.
options.B: 50% in every month.
options.C: 75% in up months and 25% in down months.

rationales.A: That is the negative asymmetry pattern: heavier participation when the index falls than when it rises gives upside capture of 25% against downside capture of 75%, a capture ratio of about 0.3, and a concave return profile. Positive asymmetry requires the opposite tilt.
rationales.B: A constant weight produces a symmetric profile, not an asymmetric one. Holding 50% of the index in every month captures half of each move in either direction, so upside capture of 50% and downside capture of 50% give a capture ratio of 1.0. Asymmetry requires the allocation to depend on the sign of the index return.
rationales.C: The positive asymmetry profile is allocated 75% to the index for months when the index return is positive and 25% when the index return is negative, with the remainder allocated to 90-day Treasury bills. Participating in three-quarters of the gains and only a quarter of the losses produces upside capture of 75%, downside capture of 25%, and a capture ratio of 3.0, which is a convex return profile. Measured over a long sample such as January 2000 to December 2013, it is the state-dependent allocation that generates the asymmetry; a fixed weight cannot.

questions.stem: Comparing a long-only profile with a low-beta profile, the most likely accurate statement is that:

options.A: the long-only profile is fully invested in the index throughout the period.
options.B: the long-only profile shifts between the index and bills with the market's sign.
options.C: the low-beta profile holds the index only in down months.

rationales.A: The long-only profile is 100% allocated to the index throughout the period, while the low-beta profile is allocated 50% to the index throughout the period. Both are static allocations, so both participate proportionally in market moves in either direction: upside capture 100% and downside capture 100% for long only, upside capture 50% and downside capture 50% for low beta. Each therefore has a capture ratio of 1.0, a symmetric return profile; the low-beta profile simply delivers lower absolute return and lower absolute risk.
rationales.B: A long-only profile does not time the market: it stays fully invested in the index in every month, up or down. The profiles that shift between the index and Treasury bills according to the sign of the market return are the asymmetry profiles, and that shifting is what gives them a capture ratio other than 1.0.
rationales.C: The low-beta profile holds 50% in the index throughout the period, in up months and down months alike. That constant weight is what makes its captures symmetric at 50% each, for a capture ratio of 1.0. A weight applied only in down months would raise participation in losses relative to gains and produce negative asymmetry instead.

questions.curriculum_ref: Capture/Drawdown — long only vs low beta

questions.stem: When capture ratios and drawdown measures are used together in manager selection, they most likely:

options.A: capture the same property, so that using both is redundant.
options.B: describe complementary effects on return performance.
options.C: are superseded by drawdown analysis for asymmetric strategies.

rationales.A: The two are complementary lenses rather than one measure counted twice. Capture ratios describe participation in up and down markets, which is the shape, or asymmetry, of the return pattern; drawdown describes the depth of the cumulative peak-to-trough loss and the time taken to recover it. A manager can show a favorable capture ratio and still have suffered a deep and slow drawdown.
rationales.B: Stylized trading strategies are designed precisely to illustrate the potential effects of the capture ratio and of drawdown on return performance, and to highlight why understanding the capture ratio and drawdown is important for manager selection. An asymmetrical return profile, or the avoidance of large drawdowns, particularly during periods when the market is not trending strongly upward, can result in higher risk-adjusted returns. A sample period such as 2000 through 2013 is chosen for that demonstration because it encompasses the extreme drawdown of 2008 and 2009, when the gap between a symmetric profile and a convex one is widest.
rationales.C: Neither measure replaces the other, least of all for asymmetric strategies, where both are needed: the capture ratio shows how much of the benchmark's upside and downside the manager takes on, and the drawdown statistics show how deep the resulting losses ran and how long recovery took.

questions.stem: A classification of active equity managers by tracking risk and diversification is most likely to show that:

options.A: tracking risk is unobservable, so no such classification is possible.
options.B: closet indexers have high tracking risk and high diversification.
options.C: concentrated stock pickers have high tracking risk and low diversification.

rationales.A: Tracking risk is directly measurable from the variability of a portfolio's return differences against its benchmark, and it forms one of the two axes of the classification; diversification forms the other. Because both dimensions are observable, manager types can be sorted into quadrants.
rationales.B: Closet indexers sit in the low-tracking-risk quadrant: they claim to be active but hold portfolios close enough to the benchmark that active risk stays small. High tracking risk combined with low diversification describes concentrated stock pickers, not closet indexers.
rationales.C: The framework sorts managers on two dimensions, tracking risk (high or low) and diversification (high or low). Sector rotators concentrate their bets across sectors, which gives high tracking risk and low diversification across sectors. Concentrated stock pickers concentrate the stock picks themselves, holding few positions, which gives high tracking risk and low diversification of holdings. Closet indexers deliver low tracking risk despite claiming to be active. Diversified stock pickers spread many small active bets, which keeps tracking risk lower.

drills.los_text: evaluate a manager's investment philosophy and investment decision-making process

questions.stem: A manager's investment philosophy is most likely:

options.A: the foundation of the investment process.
options.B: the set of trading rules that assigns each security a target weight.
options.C: the marketing statement a firm uses to differentiate itself from competitors.

rationales.A: The investment philosophy is the foundation of the investment process. Every investment strategy rests on a set of assumptions about the factors that drive performance and on the manager's beliefs about the ability to exploit those sources of return, so the manager should hold a clear and concise investment philosophy. Every manager makes assumptions about market efficiency, including its degree and its time frame: index-based strategies assume markets are sufficiently efficient that active management cannot add value after transaction costs and fees, while active strategies assume mispricings can be identified and exploited.
rationales.B: A detailed set of trading rules that assigns each security a target weight describes portfolio construction, an element of the investment process that sits downstream of the philosophy. The philosophy is the underlying set of beliefs about the sources of return that the process is built to exploit.
rationales.C: The philosophy is the substantive foundation of a strategy: the assumptions about market efficiency and about what drives returns. It is not a marketing device, and a statement written to differentiate a firm competitively says nothing about the assumptions underpinning the process.

questions.stem: The distinction between behavioral and structural inefficiencies is most likely that:

options.A: the two are one category, since all mispricings trace to investor psychology.
options.B: structural inefficiencies arise from biases such as trend following and loss aversion.
options.C: behavioral inefficiencies arise from biases such as trend following and loss aversion.

rationales.A: The two are distinct categories. Behavioral inefficiencies come from the actions and biases of other market participants, while structural inefficiencies come from external or internal rules, regulation, and market design. Not every mispricing traces to investor psychology, which is why the two categories carry different expected lives.
rationales.B: Mispricings driven by biases such as trend following and loss aversion are behavioral, not structural. Structural inefficiencies are perceived mispricings created by external or internal rules and regulations, which is why they can be long lived rather than temporary.
rationales.C: Active strategies assume markets are sufficiently inefficient that security mispricings can be identified and exploited, and those opportunities typically arise when market behavior deviates from the manager's fundamental assumptions. Inefficiencies are generally categorized as behavioral or structural. Behavioral inefficiencies are perceived mispricings created by the actions of other market participants, usually associated with biases such as trend following or loss aversion; they are temporary, lasting long enough for the manager to identify and exploit them before market price and perceived intrinsic value converge. Structural inefficiencies are perceived mispricings created by external or internal rules and regulations; they can be long lived and assume a continuation of those rules and regulations rather than a convergence.

questions.stem: A question used to evaluate a manager's investment philosophy is most likely:

options.A: whether the manager articulates the philosophy clearly and consistently.
options.B: whether investment personnel have the expertise to implement the process.
options.C: whether the philosophy is updated often in response to flows and performance.

rationales.A: Whether the manager can clearly and consistently articulate the investment philosophy is the first question asked: it is hard to have confidence in the repeatability and efficacy of an investment process if the manager and the investment personnel cannot explain the assumptions that underpin it. The related questions are whether those assumptions are credible and consistent, meaning the decision maker agrees with them and they fit the investment process; how the philosophy has developed over time; and whether the sources of return are linked to credible and consistent inefficiencies, whether informational, behavioral, or structural.
rationales.B: Whether the investment personnel possess the expertise and experience to implement the process is a question about people, not about philosophy. The philosophy questions concern clear and consistent articulation, credible and consistent assumptions, how the philosophy developed over time, and return sources linked to credible inefficiencies.
rationales.C: The ideal is a philosophy that is unchanged through time, which suggests a repeatable process. Where the philosophy has evolved, the changes should be judged reasonable responses to changing market conditions; frequent revisions driven by recent performance or investor flows are a series of ad hoc reactions and a warning sign, not something an evaluator looks for.

questions.stem: The capacity of an inefficiency a manager seeks to exploit is most likely:

options.A: the assets it can absorb without diluting returns, the opportunity set, and liquidity.
options.B: unlimited when the manager trades liquid large-cap securities.
options.C: a function of the manager's current assets under management alone.

rationales.A: Where the source of return is linked to a credible inefficiency, capacity becomes the additional issue, and it has several related aspects: the level of assets the strategy or opportunity can absorb without a dilution of returns, the number of opportunities or securities available, and the ability to transact in a timely manner at or near the market price, that is, liquidity. Overall, capacity is the level, repeatability, and sustainability of returns the inefficiency is expected to support in the future. The key questions are whether the inefficiency provides a sufficient frequency of opportunity and level of return to cover transaction costs and fees, and if so whether that requires leverage; whether it provides a repeatable source of return; and whether it is sustainable, that is, at what asset level the realized return would be unacceptably low. Sustainability is a function of the market's depth and liquidity as well as how much capital is allocated to the inefficiency by the manager or by competitors: all else equal, the more well known an inefficiency, the more likely it is to be arbitraged away.
rationales.B: Liquidity in large-cap securities raises capacity but does not make it unlimited. Returns dilute as assets grow relative to the opportunity set, and a well-known inefficiency attracts competing capital that arbitrages it away.
rationales.C: Current assets under management are only a starting point. Capacity spans the assets the opportunity can absorb without a dilution of returns, the number of opportunities or securities available, and the ability to transact in a timely manner at or near the market price.

questions.stem: Signal creation within a manager's investment decision-making process is most likely:

options.A: the identification of data observable early enough to implement as a position.
options.B: the execution of trades once a target position size has been determined.
options.C: the review of existing positions against portfolio risk limits and guidelines.

rationales.A: An investment signal is a data point or fact that can be observed early enough to implement as an investment position, so signal creation answers the question of how investment ideas are generated. The efficient market hypothesis posits that the key to exploiting an inefficiency is information that is all of the following: unique, which raises how the information is collected and how the manager retains an informational edge in a regulatory environment that seeks to reduce informational asymmetries; timely, which asks whether the strategy possesses an information timing advantage; and interpreted differently, which is typically how managers seek to differentiate themselves, so the question is whether the manager has a unique way of interpreting information.
rationales.B: Executing trades once a target position size has been determined is signal capture, or idea implementation, a separate element of the decision-making process that follows signal creation.
rationales.C: Reviewing existing positions against risk limits and guidelines is portfolio monitoring, another element of the decision-making process, distinct from the generation of the ideas themselves.

questions.stem: The four elements of a manager's investment decision-making process are most likely:

options.A: philosophy, process, people, and portfolio construction.
options.B: signal creation, signal capture, portfolio construction, and portfolio monitoring.
options.C: universe definition, quantitative analysis, qualitative analysis, and monitoring.

rationales.A: Philosophy, process, people, and portfolio construction are aspects of investment due diligence performed on a manager, not the elements of the manager's own decision-making process, which are signal creation, signal capture, portfolio construction, and portfolio monitoring.
rationales.B: The investment decision-making process has four elements: signal creation, or idea generation; signal capture, or idea implementation; portfolio construction; and portfolio monitoring.
rationales.C: Universe definition, quantitative analysis, qualitative analysis, and monitoring are components of the manager search and selection process run by the asset owner, not elements of the manager's investment decision-making process.

questions.stem: In evaluating a manager's portfolio construction, the review is most likely:

options.A: unnecessary when the manager's philosophy is well articulated.
options.B: limited to verifying position counts against the prospectus.
options.C: focused on how portfolio allocations are set and adjusted.

rationales.A: An articulated philosophy is only a claim; it has to be tested against how allocations are actually set and adjusted. Consistency between the stated philosophy and process on one side and the resulting portfolio on the other is exactly what the construction review examines.
rationales.B: Counting positions against the prospectus is not the inquiry. The review is substantive: how allocations are determined and adjusted, whether they reflect conviction, how the portfolio has changed with asset growth, how risk is managed, and what securities are used.
rationales.C: The central question is how portfolio allocations are set and adjusted, because the allocation process should be consistent with the investment philosophy and process. For an actively managed portfolio, turnover should agree with the frequency of the signals, the payoff horizon of the signals, and the securities' liquidity. The related questions are whether allocations incorporate the manager's conviction rather than only the securities' risks and correlations with other holdings; how portfolio characteristics have changed with asset growth, including whether the number or character of positions changed to accommodate larger assets under management; whether the portfolio uses stop-losses to manage risk, and if so whether they are hard, with positions automatically sold when the loss threshold is reached, or soft, with positions evaluated when that threshold is reached; and what types of securities are used.

questions.stem: In evaluating a manager's investment personnel, the inquiry is most likely:

options.A: relevant only for quantitative strategies that depend on model expertise.
options.B: limited to confirming professional certifications and degrees.
options.C: focused on whether the team can execute the investment process.

rationales.A: Every strategy depends on the people executing it, quantitative or discretionary, so the personnel evaluation applies universally rather than only where model expertise is central.
rationales.B: Credentials are a fraction of the assessment. The question is whether the team's expertise and experience are sufficient to execute the investment process, including through personnel change, and whether depth, incentives, and turnover support that over time.
rationales.C: The central question is whether the investment team has sufficient expertise and experience to execute the investment process effectively. The need for expertise is self-evident, and the greater the experience, particularly managing the current strategy across market environments, the greater the confidence in the manager's ability to execute; as with drawdowns, it is especially instructive to see how the manager responded to stressed markets and poor performance. The related questions are whether the team has sufficient depth to execute the process; what the level of key person risk is, meaning an overreliance on an individual or small team whose departure would negatively affect the strategy's performance; what agreements, such as non-competes, and what incentives, such as ownership, bonus, and pay, exist to attract key employees and keep them at the firm; and what the turnover of firm personnel has been, since high turnover risks the loss of institutional knowledge and experience within the team.

drills.los_text: discuss how behavioral factors affect investment team decision making, and recommend techniques for mitigating their effects

questions.stem: Among US active mutual funds, team-managed funds are most likely to:

options.A: outperform individually managed funds.
options.B: make up a majority of those funds.
options.C: make up a minority of those funds.

rationales.A: The research is mixed rather than consistent: several studies find team-managed funds underperform individually managed funds, several find the opposite, and some find no difference. There is nothing magical about a team, so managers should focus on creating an effective structure and culture.
rationales.B: Investment decisions are often made by teams rather than individuals, and in 2021 team-managed mutual funds accounted for 64% of all US active mutual funds (Karagiannidis and Booth 2022), a majority. The primary motivation for team management is the idea that two heads are better than one: applying to a task a number of individuals, each with different skills and experiences, can provide for more effective decision making. A secondary motivation is to mitigate key person risk. While teams can mitigate some individual behavioral biases, such as overconfidence in forecasting, they also introduce new biases or exacerbate others.
rationales.C: Team management is the majority case, not a minority one: team-managed funds accounted for 64% of all US active mutual funds in 2021, so a share of roughly a quarter understates their prevalence substantially.

questions.stem: Three common behavioral biases that adversely affect investment team performance are most likely:

options.A: Overconfidence, loss aversion, and anchoring.
options.B: Groupthink, trend following, and regret aversion.
options.C: Groupthink, authority bias, and aversion to complexity.

rationales.A: Overconfidence, loss aversion, and anchoring are biases of individual investors rather than the team-level biases identified for investment teams. The three team biases are groupthink, authority bias, and aversion to complexity.
rationales.B: Only groupthink belongs on the list. The other two team biases are authority bias and aversion to complexity, not trend following or regret aversion, which are individual-level behaviors.
rationales.C: The three common behavioral biases that can adversely affect investment teams' performance are groupthink, authority bias, and aversion to complexity. Groupthink occurs when a team minimizes conflict and dissent in reaching and maintaining a consensus. Authority bias involves the group deferring to a member who is a subject matter expert or in a position of authority, such as the senior-most member. Aversion to complexity is the phenomenon in which disproportionate attention is given to trivial issues at the expense of important but harder-to-grasp or contested topics.

questions.stem: Groupthink is most likely characterized by a team:

options.A: Deferring to its senior-most member or subject matter expert.
options.B: Minimizing conflict and dissent to reach and maintain a consensus.
options.C: Devoting disproportionate time to trivial rather than important issues.

rationales.A: Deferring to the senior-most member or to the subject matter expert describes authority bias, not groupthink. The two differ in what suppresses dissent: in authority bias it is the standing of one member, whereas in groupthink it is the team's own pursuit of harmony.
rationales.B: Groupthink occurs when a team minimizes conflict and dissent in reaching and maintaining a consensus. The pursuit of harmony overrides individual expression and may even encourage individuals to withhold information and their perspectives from the team. Common symptoms of groupthink are closed-mindedness and confirmation bias, where fresh sources of information, different interpretations, and dissent are ignored or minimized. For example, a portfolio management team may become convinced that a recession is imminent on the basis of an inverted yield curve and falling commodity prices and thus seek to position the portfolio defensively by decreasing exposure to cyclicals. While this may ultimately be the right decision, the team must remain open to the possibility that it is not.
rationales.C: Devoting disproportionate time to trivial rather than important issues describes aversion to complexity, colloquially known as bike-shedding, not groupthink.

questions.stem: Authority bias is most likely characterized by:

options.A: Junior analysts overstating their own expertise to gain influence.
options.B: Groups rejecting expert opinion in favor of consensus.
options.C: Groups deferring to a subject matter expert or senior-most member.

rationales.A: The bias is the group's deference to the authority figure or subject matter expert, not self-promotion by a junior member. Nothing in the bias turns on how a junior analyst represents their own expertise.
rationales.B: The failure runs toward the authority, not against it: the group defers to the expert's view rather than challenging it. A group that rejected expert opinion in order to preserve agreement would be closer to groupthink, and even then the mechanism would be harmony seeking rather than deference.
rationales.C: Authority bias involves groups deferring to a group member who is a subject matter expert or in a position of authority, such as the senior-most group member. For example, a research analyst may recommend a semiconductor equipment stock to a team of three portfolio managers. One of the portfolio managers is a former technology research analyst and votes not to buy the stock. The other two members vote the same way, deferring to the subject matter expertise of the other manager. While this may be the right call, it undermines the reason for a team in the first place: a synthesis of diverse perspectives and skills.

questions.stem: Aversion to complexity, also known as bike-shedding, is most likely characterized by:

options.A: Disproportionate attention to trivial issues at the expense of important ones.
options.B: Excessive committee time spent on the most complex agenda items.
options.C: Work expanding to fill the time allotted to it.

rationales.A: Aversion to complexity is a well-known phenomenon of groups in many professional contexts, in which disproportionate attention is given to trivial issues at the expense of important but harder-to-grasp or contested topics. It is also known as Parkinson's law of triviality or, colloquially, bike-shedding, after C. Northcote Parkinson's 1957 story of a hypothetical committee organized to approve plans for a nuclear power plant that spent more time discussing the design of a bicycle storage shed outside the plant than the design of the nuclear reactor. A survey of more than 120 investment committees asked members to rank their tasks from most to least important and then to track how they actually allocated their time; the committees spent a great deal of time on issues they rated as unimportant, at the expense of important and more difficult issues such as asset allocation, capital market expectations, and manager selection (Payne and Wood 2002).
rationales.B: The phenomenon runs in the reverse direction: attention flows disproportionately to trivial, easy-to-grasp issues, and the important but harder or more contested topics are the ones that get crowded out.
rationales.C: Work expanding to fill the time allotted is Parkinson's law. The law of triviality, or bike-shedding, is a different proposition about where a group's attention goes, namely toward the trivial topics rather than the difficult ones.

questions.stem: Techniques for mitigating investment team biases most likely include:

options.A: Making the team as large as possible, well beyond five members.
options.B: Assigning every decision to one accountable individual.
options.C: Keeping the team to between three and five members.

rationales.A: Larger teams introduce too many coordination issues and increase the odds of groupthink, so expanding the team does not dilute bias. Research suggests a team size of three to five is optimal (Patel and Sarkissian 2017).
rationales.B: Concentrating every decision in one person trades group biases for individual ones and forfeits the synthesis of diverse perspectives that is the reason for having a team. The recommended techniques work on the structure and conduct of a small team instead.
rationales.C: Research suggests that a team size between three and five is optimal, with larger teams introducing too many coordination issues (Patel and Sarkissian 2017) and increasing the odds of groupthink. Other mitigation techniques concern how decisions are made and how meetings are run. While it may be awkward, using a secret ballot may be preferable to open deliberation because it reduces groupthink and authority bias. To avoid complexity aversion, as well as availability bias, meeting agendas should be agreed on in advance, with the most important topics covered first and allotted the longest time for discussion. Team diversity, in social and cognitive categories, can also reduce groupthink and errors, which is among the reasons CFA Institute has long advocated for diversity, equity, and inclusion in the investment industry.

questions.stem: Research on social and cognitive diversity in investment teams most likely finds that diversity:

options.A: Reduces groupthink and errors, as uncorrelated assets reduce portfolio volatility.
options.B: Reduces errors through a mechanism with no analogue in portfolio theory.
options.C: Increases groupthink by impeding shared understanding.

rationales.A: Research suggests that team diversity, in terms of social and cognitive categories, can reduce groupthink and errors, analogous to how combinations of uncorrelated assets reduce portfolio volatility. It also suggests that members of diverse teams may devote more effort to tasks because they are less concerned with socially fitting in and with the conflict avoidance that is common in homogeneous groups. For these reasons and others, CFA Institute has long advocated for diversity, equity, and inclusion in the investment industry.
rationales.B: The benefit is explained by precisely such an analogue: imperfectly correlated perspectives, like imperfectly correlated assets, reduce aggregate error, which is the diversification argument carried over from portfolio construction. The finding is therefore not an isolated empirical result.
rationales.C: Social and cognitive diversity reduces groupthink and errors rather than increasing them. Diverse teams are less exposed to the harmony seeking and conflict avoidance common in homogeneous groups, and their members may devote more effort to tasks because they are less concerned with socially fitting in.

questions.stem: Research on how investment committees allocate their meeting time most likely shows that committees:

options.A: Allocate time in close proportion to their own importance rankings.
options.B: Have not been studied on this question.
options.C: Spend substantial time on issues they rate as unimportant.

rationales.A: The survey evidence documents misalignment, not alignment. Time flowed toward the issues members themselves had ranked as less important, and away from the important and more difficult ones.
rationales.B: Such research exists: a survey of more than 120 investment committees addressed exactly this question, and it documented the misalignment between ranked importance and actual time use.
rationales.C: A survey of more than 120 investment committees asked committee members to rank their tasks from most to least important and then asked the members to keep track of how they actually allocated their time. The survey revealed that the committees spent a great deal of time on issues they rated as unimportant, at the expense of important and more difficult issues, such as asset allocation, capital market expectations, and manager selection (Payne and Wood 2002). This is aversion to complexity at the committee level, and the mitigation is to agree the agenda in advance, with the most important topics covered first and allotted the longest time for discussion.

drills.los_text: evaluate the costs and benefits of pooled investment vehicles and separate accounts

questions.stem: The two broad options for implementing an investment strategy are most likely:

options.A: Active mandates and passive mandates.
options.B: Individual separate accounts and pooled (commingled) vehicles.
options.C: Open-end funds and closed-end funds.

rationales.A: Active versus passive is a strategy decision taken when the manager universe is defined, not a choice of implementation structure. The two broad options for implementing a strategy are individual separate accounts and pooled (commingled) vehicles, and either can hold an active or a passive mandate.
rationales.B: There are two broad options for implementing investment strategies: individual separate accounts and pooled (or commingled) vehicles. Separate accounts offer additional control, customization, tax efficiency, reporting, and transparency advantages, but these come at a higher cost. In a pooled or commingled vehicle, the money from multiple investors is held as a single portfolio and managed without potential customization for any investor; such vehicles include open-end funds, closed-end funds, exchange-traded funds, exchange-traded notes, and hedge funds. An additional operational consideration is the evaluation of the investment vehicle itself, meaning its appropriateness to the investment strategy and its suitability for the investor.
rationales.C: Open-end and closed-end funds are both examples of pooled (commingled) vehicles, alongside exchange-traded funds, exchange-traded notes, and hedge funds. They sit within one of the two broad options; the other is the individual separate account.

questions.stem: Compared with a pooled vehicle, a separately managed account most likely offers:

options.A: Lower cost than any pooled alternative.
options.B: Direct ownership of the individual securities.
options.C: No substantive advantage beyond prestige.

rationales.A: Separate accounts represent an additional operational burden on the manager, which translates into potentially higher costs for the investor, and they do not scale as pooled vehicles do. Cost is therefore a disadvantage of the structure; its advantages are ownership, customization, tax efficiency, and transparency.
rationales.B: In a separately managed account the investor owns the individual securities directly. This provides additional safety should a liquidity event occur: although the manager continues to make investment decisions, those decisions will not be influenced by the redemption or liquidity demand of other investors in the strategy, and the structure provides clear legal ownership for the recovery of assets resulting from unforeseen events such as bankruptcy or mismanagement. The other advantages are customization, which allows the investor to express individual constraints or preferences within the portfolio; tax efficiency, in jurisdictions such as the United States where investors pay taxes only on realized capital gains; and transparency, since real-time position-level detail gives complete transparency and accurate attribution, whereas a pooled vehicle that discloses positions will likely do so with a delay.
rationales.C: The structure confers substantive advantages, not merely standing: direct ownership of the securities, insulation from other investors' redemption and liquidity demands, customization to the investor's constraints, potential tax efficiency, and real-time position-level transparency.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of a separately managed account relative to a pooled vehicle is most likely:

options.A: Reduced tracking risk owing to customization.
options.B: Lower transaction costs from aggregating trades.
options.C: Higher cost from the added operational burden.

rationales.A: Customization of the strategy creates tracking risk relative to the benchmark rather than reducing it, and that tracking risk can confuse attribution, because performance will reflect investor constraints rather than manager decisions.
rationales.B: This reverses the position: separately managed accounts are likely to face higher transaction costs to the degree that trades cannot be aggregated to reduce trade volumes. Pooled vehicles are the structure in which trading is aggregated across investors.
rationales.C: Separate accounts represent an additional operational burden on the manager, which translates into potentially higher costs for the investor. They do not scale as easily as pooled vehicles: once a pooled investment is established and the fixed costs paid, the cost of each new investor is largely the incremental cost of custody, trading larger positions, and generating an additional report, whereas with a separately managed account a new account must be established for each investor. They are also likely to face higher transaction costs to the degree that trades cannot be aggregated. The other disadvantages are tracking risk, since customization creates tracking risk relative to the benchmark and can confuse attribution, and investor behavior, since transparency combined with control and customization allows for potential micromanagement, including performance chasing, familiarity bias, and loss aversion.

questions.stem: When an allocator evaluates an SMA against a pooled vehicle, the evaluation is most likely to center on:

options.A: whether the vehicle structure is consistent with the investment process.
options.B: whether the SMA charges a lower headline fee than the pooled fund.
options.C: whether the manager's past returns exceed the pooled vehicle's.

rationales.A: The allocator's goal is to evaluate the costs and benefits of the vehicle used and judge its suitability for the IPS. That evaluation asks: Is the vehicle structure consistent with the investment process? Does the manager have the operational infrastructure necessary to manage the SMA?
