Is there a benefit to holding the securities in a separate account, and if so, are those benefits sufficient to compensate for the additional costs? Is tax efficiency an important objective of the IPS? Are there concerns that the available transparency and ability to customize will result in decisions by the investor that do not add value? Consistency between vehicle structure and investment process is the first of these questions and the frame for the rest.
rationales.B: Cost is only one factor in the evaluation. The allocator also weighs the manager's operational infrastructure for running separate accounts, the importance of tax efficiency to the IPS, the benefits of holding securities directly against the additional costs of doing so, and the risk that transparency and the ability to customize lead the investor into decisions that do not add value. A lower headline fee on its own does not establish that the vehicle suits the IPS.
rationales.C: The evaluation concerns the suitability of the vehicle to the IPS and to the manager's investment process, not a return comparison between vehicles. Relative past returns say nothing about whether the structure fits the investment process, whether the operational infrastructure to run an SMA exists, whether direct ownership and tax efficiency matter to this investor, or whether customization and transparency will tempt the investor into value-destroying decisions.

questions.stem: Among pooled investment vehicles, the most liquid are most likely:

options.A: closed-end funds and ETFs.
options.B: limited partnerships.
options.C: open-end mutual funds.

rationales.A: The most liquid vehicles are closed-end funds and ETFs. As listed securities they can be bought and sold intra-day, and the price received depends on the trading volume and depth of the fund. The obvious advantage is ease of trading, although there can be some price uncertainty for less liquid funds, particularly when trying to buy or sell a large number of shares. Open-end funds are slightly less liquid: they provide daily liquidity but also price certainty, since shares are bought and sold at the end-of-day NAV.
rationales.B: Limited partnerships sit at the illiquid end of the range rather than leading on liquidity. Capital is committed through capital calls, and the ability to get it back is constrained by lockups and gates rather than served by any regular dealing window. Partnerships provide the least liquidity of the pooled vehicles.
rationales.C: Open-end mutual funds are slightly less liquid than exchange-listed funds. They offer daily liquidity at the end-of-day NAV, which brings price certainty but only one dealing point per day, whereas closed-end funds and ETFs trade continuously intra-day as listed securities.

questions.stem: Hedge fund liquidity is most likely characterized by:

options.A: four features: redemption frequency, notification period, lockup, and gates.
options.B: three features: lockup, high-water mark, and capital calls.
options.C: two features: redemption frequency and management fee level.

rationales.A: Hedge fund liquidity has four basic features. Redemption frequency is how often an investor can withdraw capital from the fund. The notification period is how far in advance of the redemption investors must tell the fund of their intention to redeem. A lockup is the initial period, after making an investment, during which investors cannot redeem their holding; a hard lock allows no redemptions, while a soft lock charges a fee, paid into the fund, for redemptions, which makes a mutual fund redemption fee the equivalent of a hedge fund soft lock. Gates limit the amount of fund assets, or of investor assets, that can be redeemed at one redemption date.
rationales.B: A lockup is indeed one of the liquidity features, but a high-water mark is a fee feature governing when incentive fees are earned, and capital calls are a private equity feature of committed capital. The four liquidity features are redemption frequency, notification period, lockup, and gates.
rationales.C: Redemption frequency is one of the features, but the management fee level is a fee term rather than a liquidity term, and two understates the list. The four liquidity features are redemption frequency, notification period, lockup, and gates, the last two of which can block redemption entirely for a period or cap the amount redeemable on a given date.

questions.stem: Partnership liquidity terms in private equity and venture capital funds are most likely to provide:

options.A: the greatest liquidity of any pooled vehicle.
options.B: the least liquidity of any pooled vehicle.
options.C: quarterly redemptions subject to a notification period.

rationales.A: Private equity and venture capital funds provide the least, not the greatest, liquidity. Capital is not recycled on demand: investors are contractually obligated to contribute specific amounts through capital calls during an investment phase that typically runs 5 years, and receive capital back only as distributions when investments are harvested over the remaining term, with a typical fund life of 10 years and an option to extend for two 1-year periods.
rationales.B: Private equity and venture capital funds provide the least liquidity. Investors are contractually obligated to contribute specific amounts (capital calls) during the investment phase and then receive distributions and capital as investments are harvested during the remaining term of the fund. A typical investment phase is 5 years; the typical life of a fund is 10 years, with the option to extend the term for two 1-year periods. The disadvantage of these terms is reduced flexibility to adjust portfolio allocations and reduced ability to meet unexpected liquidity needs. The advantage is that they lock up capital for longer horizons, allowing funds to take long-term views and hold less liquid securities such as start-ups, buyouts, turnarounds, real estate, and natural resources with reduced risk of having to sell holdings at inopportune times.
rationales.C: Quarterly redemption subject to a notification period describes hedge fund style liquidity terms, not partnership terms. Private equity and venture capital capital is drawn through capital calls and returned through distributions as investments are harvested; there are no interim redemption dates during the roughly 10-year fund life.

questions.stem: Liquidity for an investor in a separately managed account is most likely:

options.A: determined by the liquidity of the securities held.
options.B: set by the redemption schedule in the SMA agreement.
options.C: uniformly high regardless of the securities held.

rationales.A: Because SMA assets are held in the investor's name, the securities in the portfolio can be sold at any time. As a result, an SMA's liquidity will depend on the liquidity of the securities held: an SMA holding listed large-cap stocks will likely be highly liquid, whereas an investor in an SMA that holds unlisted or illiquid securities will have to accept a discount when selling.
rationales.B: An SMA imposes no redemption schedule, monthly, quarterly or otherwise. Direct ownership in the investor's name means the holdings can be sold at any time, so liquidity tracks the underlying securities rather than a dealing calendar imposed by a vehicle; redemption frequency and notification periods are features of pooled funds and partnerships.
rationales.C: Liquidity is not uniform across separate accounts, because the mandate determines what is held. An SMA of listed large-cap equities is likely to be highly liquid, but one holding unlisted or illiquid securities would force the investor to accept a discount when selling, so the vehicle's form alone does not guarantee high liquidity.

drills.los_text: compare types of investment manager contracts, including their major provisions and advantages and disadvantages

questions.stem: The contract between an investor and an investment manager is most likely set out in:

options.A: the prospectus, private placement memorandum, or limited partnership agreement.
options.B: informal understandings rather than any offering document.
options.C: the investment policy statement alone.

rationales.A: An important aspect of manager selection is understanding the terms of the investment as presented in the prospectus, private placement memorandum, and/or limited partnership agreement. These documents are, in essence, the contract between the investor and the manager, outlining each party's rights and responsibilities. They cover numerous topics, but liquidity and fees are the focus of the evaluation: the objective of the decision maker is to determine whether the liquidity and fee structure make the manager suitable for the investor's needs and the best manager for expressing a particular portfolio need.
rationales.B: The relationship is documented rather than informal. The prospectus, private placement memorandum, and/or limited partnership agreement function as the contract that defines each party's rights and responsibilities, and they are where the liquidity and fee terms the allocator evaluates are actually specified.
rationales.C: The IPS governs the advisory relationship and records the investor's objectives and constraints; it is not the contract for every vehicle type. Pooled funds and partnerships are governed by their own offering and partnership documents, which set out redemption terms, lockups, gates and fee structures.

questions.stem: Of the effects of partnership liquidity terms, the disadvantage to investors is most likely:

options.A: lost flexibility to adjust allocations and meet unexpected needs.
options.B: protection from panic selling.
options.C: fee discounts granted in exchange for the lockup.

rationales.A: The obvious disadvantage of partnership liquidity terms is the reduced flexibility to adjust portfolio allocations in light of changing market conditions or investor circumstances, as well as the reduced ability to meet unexpected liquidity needs. The advantage of such terms is that they lock up capital for longer horizons, allowing funds to take long-term views and hold less liquid securities such as start-up companies, buyouts, turnarounds, real estate or natural resources, with reduced risk of having to sell portfolio holdings at inopportune times in response to redemption requests. A further advantage, apparent during the 2008 financial crisis, is that limited liquidity imposes this long-horizon view on investors, reducing or removing their ability to overreact.
rationales.B: Whatever behavioral benefit the lockup brings, it is listed among the advantages of these terms rather than the disadvantage. Limited liquidity imposes a long-horizon view and removes the ability to overreact, as was apparent during the 2008 financial crisis. The disadvantage is the loss of flexibility to adjust allocations as conditions or circumstances change and the reduced ability to meet unexpected liquidity needs.
rationales.C: No automatic fee compensation accompanies partnership liquidity terms, and even where fees are negotiated lower the cost of the terms remains real: allocations cannot be adjusted in light of changing market conditions or investor circumstances, and unexpected liquidity needs cannot be met from committed capital.

questions.stem: Assets under management fees are most likely:

options.A: a fixed amount set at inception, independent of asset values.
options.B: a stated percentage applied to assets under management.
options.C: a percentage of profit earned above a stated hurdle rate.

rationales.A: Ad valorem fees are not a fixed amount agreed at inception. They apply stated percentage rates to assets under management, so the fee varies directly with asset values and rises as the portfolio rises, including when the increase comes from the market rather than from the manager.
rationales.B: Assets under management fees, also called ad valorem fees from the Latin for according to value, result from applying stated percentage rates to assets under management. These fees reward managers who attract and retain assets, generate added value, and experience benefits from rising markets. Managers primarily grow their assets through skillful investing, hard work and effective marketing, but a manager's success also results partly from luck, especially in the short term: managers benefit from rising portfolio values, which are attributable to the combination of alpha and beta decisions but are also, at least for long-only managers, greatly affected by market cycles beyond the manager's control. A decline in ad valorem percentages as assets grow helps reduce the fee impact on investors from rising markets, but does not eliminate it.
rationales.C: A percentage charged on profit above a stated hurdle is a performance or incentive fee, which depends on returns earned. An ad valorem fee applies its percentage to total assets under management whether or not any profit is earned.

questions.stem: A manager whose assets under management have grown large is most likely to:

options.A: need continued outperformance to retain those assets.
options.B: take greater active risk to retain those assets.
options.C: avoid active risk that could jeopardize those assets.

rationales.A: Assets are typically sticky, so flows do not leave rapidly on the back of weaker performance, and empirical evidence suggests this is the case, to some extent, for mutual fund assets. Once investors have allocated to a manager, the manager often does not need to generate the same level of returns to retain the assets as was needed to attract them, so continued outperformance is not the condition for keeping them.
rationales.B: Stickiness cuts the other way. Because a large manager needs less return to retain assets than was needed to attract them, the incentive is to reduce active risk and closet index rather than to take more risk. That is precisely why an incentive fee determined by future performance may be useful: to motivate such managers to work harder or to discourage them from closet indexing.
rationales.C: Once a manager's assets are large, he or she might not want to risk losing them. Assets are typically sticky: once investors allocate their assets to a manager, the manager often does not need to generate the same level of returns to retain the assets as he or she did to attract them, and empirical evidence suggests this is the case, to some extent, for mutual fund assets. That reluctance to jeopardize a large asset base is the incentive behind closet indexing. To motivate such managers to work harder, or to discourage them from closet indexing, an incentive fee determined by future performance may be useful.

questions.stem: From 2000 to 2021, the average asset-weighted expense ratio paid by equity mutual fund investors is most likely to have:

options.A: fallen by roughly half.
options.B: risen slightly.
options.C: fallen by roughly a third.

rationales.A: Investors are increasingly sensitive to management fees, and average asset-weighted expense ratios, covering management fees and fund expenses, incurred by mutual fund investors have fallen substantially. In 2000, equity mutual fund investors incurred expense ratios of 0.99% on average, or 99 cents for every $100 invested. By 2021 that average had fallen to 0.47%, a decline of 53%, or roughly half. Hybrid and bond mutual fund expense ratios also declined: the average hybrid fund ratio fell from 0.89% in 2000 to 0.57% in 2021, a reduction of 36%, and the average bond fund ratio from 0.76% to 0.39%, a decline of 49%. Within equities, the average expense ratio of actively managed equity mutual funds declined from 1.06% to 0.68%, while average expense ratios for index-based equity and bond funds declined from 27 bps and 21 bps in 2000 respectively to 6 bps each in 2021.
rationales.B: Asset-weighted expense ratios fell rather than rose. The equity average dropped from 0.99% in 2000 to 0.47% in 2021, a decline of 53%. Active fees fell too: actively managed equity funds went from 1.06% to 0.68% over the same period. Hybrid funds fell from 0.89% to 0.57%, a 36% reduction, and bond funds from 0.76% to 0.39%, a 49% decline.
rationales.C: A decline of about a third corresponds to 0.99% falling to 0.68%, but 0.68% is the 2021 average for actively managed equity funds alone, down from 1.06% in 2000. The asset-weighted average across all equity mutual funds fell from 0.99% to 0.47%, a decline of 53%, because index-based equity funds, at 6 bps in 2021 against 27 bps in 2000, pull the asset-weighted figure well below the actively managed average.

questions.stem: In the principal–agent relationship between an investor and an asset manager, fee structures are most likely to:

options.A: eliminate the problem once performance fees are included.
options.B: influence both mandate acceptance and manager behavior.
options.C: leave mandate acceptance and manager behavior unaffected.

rationales.A: Performance fees create incentive distortions of their own, such as added risk taking as a fee threshold is approached, so no standard structure fully eliminates the principal–agent problem. Incentives help ensure managers routinely act in clients' best interest, but they do not remove the misalignment that arises because the agent's skills and actions are not fully visible to the principal.
rationales.B: Fee structures can influence which managers will be willing to accept a particular investment mandate, and they can also strongly affect manager behavior. Economic theory suggests the principal–agent problem is complicated by the fact that an agent's skills and actions are not fully visible to the principal: although principals control asset availability, agents control both their expenditure of effort and portfolio risk. The agent and principal may also have different preferences, since each might care about a different time horizon and agents might not view losses the same way principals do. Finally, total performance is to some extent beyond the control of either party. As a result of these factors, the principal's and agent's interests may not be fully aligned. In reality, managers are motivated to work hard even without incentive fees, because they want to retain current clients and expand their client base and pricing power; incentives are nonetheless useful to help ensure that managers routinely act in their clients' best interest.
rationales.C: Fee design shapes which managers are willing to accept a mandate and how they behave once hired, and that is the core principal–agent channel, so fees are not neutral plumbing. Because agents control their own effort and the portfolio's risk, the terms on which they are paid feed directly into both selection and conduct.

questions.stem: A comparison of institutional and mutual fund fee practice is most likely to show that:

options.A: mutual fund fees are based on assets under management.
options.B: mutual fund fees are commonly set as minimum dollar amounts.
options.C: institutional fee percentages rise as account size grows.

rationales.A: In general, mutual fund managers charge fees based on a fund's assets under management, and some classes of mutual funds, including those with reduced fees, require minimum balances. In contrast, institutional managers frequently offer declining percentage fees on increasing account sizes for separate or commingled pool accounts, and institutional accounts frequently specify minimum account sizes or minimum dollar fees. Fixed-percentage fees facilitate managers' and investors' planning for future cash flows, whereas dollar fees are subject to the variability of asset values. An individual investor does not benefit from investing more money in a mutual fund unless the extra money qualifies the investor for a lower-fee fund class.
rationales.B: Minimum dollar fees are characteristic of institutional accounts, not of mutual funds, which charge a percentage of assets under management. Where mutual fund classes do impose a threshold, it takes the form of a minimum account balance for a reduced-fee class rather than a minimum dollar fee.
rationales.C: Institutional managers typically offer declining percentage fees on increasing account sizes for separate or commingled pool accounts, so the percentage falls rather than rises with size; what institutional accounts commonly add at the small end is a minimum account size or a minimum dollar fee.

questions.stem: An investor comparing an active strategy with a passive alternative is most likely to conclude that:

options.A: neither expenses nor added value is uncertain.
options.B: only the added value is uncertain.
options.C: only the expenses are uncertain.

rationales.A: Expenses are paid for certain, but the added value of the active strategy compared with the passive strategy is not known in advance, so the two differ in their degree of uncertainty rather than both being known. The riskier the active strategy, the greater the return volatility and the greater the volatility of the added value relative to the passive strategy.
rationales.B: Expenses are paid for certain, whereas the added value of the active strategy compared with the passive strategy is uncertain. Suppose an active strategy is expected to generate a gross return that is 2% greater than the passive strategy, but the cost of the active strategy is 2% greater than the passive strategy. A risk-averse investor would likely prefer the passive strategy: although the expected net return of the strategies is the same, the uncertainty of the outperformance would be unappealing. The riskier the active strategy, the greater the return volatility and the greater the volatility of the added value relative to the passive strategy. The significance is that the added value of the active strategy has to be sufficiently large and sufficiently certain to justify the higher cost of the strategy.
rationales.C: This reverses the relationship. Expenses are the certain cost, paid whatever the outcome, and the active strategy's added value over the passive alternative is the uncertain benefit; the more risk the active strategy takes, the more volatile that added value becomes.

drills.los_text: describe the three basic forms of performance-based fees

questions.stem: The three basic structures used for performance-based fees are most likely:

options.A: symmetrical; bonus with full upside; bonus with capped upside.
options.B: base fee only; high-water mark; clawback.
options.C: symmetrical with upside only; bonus with full downside; bonus with unlimited sharing.

rationales.A: Performance-based fees are structured in one of three basic ways. First, a symmetrical structure in which the manager is fully exposed to both the downside and the upside, where computed fee = base + sharing of performance. Second, a bonus structure in which the manager is not fully exposed to the downside but is fully exposed to the upside, where computed fee = higher of either base, or base plus sharing of positive performance. Third, a bonus structure in which the manager is not fully exposed to either the downside or the upside, where computed fee = higher of either base, or base plus sharing of performance up to a limit.
rationales.B: A base-only fee is not performance based at all, and high-water marks and clawbacks are supplemental protective terms layered onto a performance fee rather than basic forms of one. The three basic forms are symmetric sharing of performance, a bonus with full upside exposure, and a bonus whose upside sharing is capped.
rationales.C: This scrambles the exposures. The symmetrical structure is the one that exposes the manager to both the downside and the upside, with computed fee = base + sharing of performance. It is the bonus structures that limit downside exposure: the second form leaves the manager fully exposed to the upside, and the third caps the upside by sharing performance only up to a limit, so no basic form offers unlimited sharing in both directions.

questions.stem: Performance-based fees are most likely:

options.A: common among hedge funds and less so among long-only strategies.
options.B: based on total return rather than on return relative to a benchmark.
options.C: standard among long-only strategies and rare among hedge funds.

rationales.A: Performance-based fees are common for hedge funds and less common for long-only strategies. They are determined by portfolio returns and are designed to reward managers with a share of return for their skill in creating value. Performance can be calculated by using either total or relative return, and the return shared can be a percentage of total performance or of performance net of a base or fixed fee. Performance fees are paid annually or, in some cases, less frequently.
rationales.B: Performance can be calculated by using either total return or return relative to a benchmark, so total return is not the only permitted basis. The return shared can likewise be a percentage of total performance or of performance net of a base or fixed fee.
rationales.C: This reverses actual practice: performance-based fees are common for hedge funds and less common for long-only strategies, where fixed fees based on assets under management predominate.

questions.stem: Maximum fee and high-water mark provisions in a performance fee are most likely to:

options.A: require investors to pay twice for the same performance.
options.B: protect the manager's revenue in down years.
options.C: protect investors from paying for a recovery of losses.

rationales.A: A high-water mark prevents exactly that double payment: no incentive fee is earned on a recovery until prior peaks have been exceeded, so performance that merely offsets earlier underperformance is not charged for a second time.
rationales.B: These features protect investors rather than the manager. A maximum caps the fee the manager can earn, and a high-water mark or clawback withholds the fee until the negative effects of prior underperformance have been offset, so both work against the manager's revenue in and after a down year.
rationales.C: Performance fees may include maximum and high-water mark (or clawback) features that protect investors from situations such as paying for current positive performance before the negative effects of prior underperformance have been offset. Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships commonly earn performance fees on total returns and typically do not limit the amount of the performance fee. Hedge funds commonly include high-water mark features.

questions.stem: For a private equity partnership, the fee arrangement is most likely to provide that:

options.A: base fees apply to committed capital.
options.B: performance fees are paid before limited partners recover principal.
options.C: base fees apply only to invested capital.

rationales.A: For private equity partnerships, base fees are commonly applied to committed, not just invested, capital. Performance fees are earned as profits are realized and invested capital is returned to investors. A common provision that helps protect private equity limited partners, the investors, is a requirement that the limited partners receive their principal and share of profits before performance fees are distributed to the general partner, the manager.
rationales.B: The order of payment runs the other way. A common provision protecting limited partners requires that they receive their principal and their share of profits before any performance fee is distributed to the general partner, with the performance fee earned as profits are realized and capital is returned.
rationales.C: Private equity base fees are commonly charged on committed capital, so they accrue on capital the limited partners have pledged whether or not it has yet been drawn and invested in deals.

questions.stem: In option terms, a bonus-style performance fee is most likely:

options.A: a put option held by the investor on manager underperformance.
options.B: not expressible as an option position.
options.C: a manager's call on active return, struck at the base fee.

rationales.A: The optionality belongs to the manager, not the investor. A bonus-style fee gives the manager a call on a share of active return, and when active return falls short the manager simply keeps the base fee rather than making a payment to the investor, so there is no investor-held put.
rationales.B: Tradability is irrelevant to the payoff analogy. The bonus fee's payoff profile is call-like, with the base fee serving as the strike price, so the structure can be decomposed into option components even though the fee itself is not a traded claim.
rationales.C: Bonus-style fees are the close equivalent of a manager's call option on a share of active return, for which the base fee is the strike price. The option payoff is modified by a maximum fee feature, so the fee decomposes into three components: the base fee, plus a long call option on active return with a strike price equal to the minimum (base) fee, minus another and less valuable call option with a strike price equal to the maximum fee. Based on option pricing theory, higher volatility leads to higher option value, which encourages managers to assume higher portfolio risk, and this behavior has been observed in the marketplace.

questions.stem: An analysis of incentive alignment under performance-based fees is most likely to conclude that:

options.A: managers favor symmetrical fees for their limited downside.
options.B: bonus-style fees align risk and effort more closely than symmetric fees.
options.C: investor and manager incentives may still diverge.

rationales.A: Symmetrical fee structures are unpopular with managers, precisely because full exposure to the downside raises the manager's bankruptcy risk. A symmetrical structure does not limit the manager's downside; it is the bonus structures that leave the manager less than fully exposed to it.
rationales.B: The utility maximization analysis points the other way: fully symmetric fees, in which the manager is fully exposed to the downside, tend to yield closer alignment in risk and effort than bonus-style fees, whose one-sided payoff rewards added volatility.
rationales.C: Investors and managers may have different incentives when performance-based fees are used. According to a utility maximization model, fully symmetric fees, in which the manager is fully exposed to the downside, tend to yield closer alignment in risk and effort than bonus-style fees. Understandably, symmetrical fee structures are unpopular with managers because of their impact on bankruptcy risk, so the structures managers prefer are the ones that align incentives least well.

questions.stem: Performance-based fee structures are most likely to:

options.A: leave the estimated standard deviation of returns unchanged.
options.B: lead to misestimation of portfolio risk.
options.C: make downside risk appear larger than it is.

rationales.A: A management fee lowers the level of realized return without affecting the standard deviation, but a performance fee has the added effect of lowering the realized standard deviation, because it trims variability on the upside while leaving the downside intact. The net return series therefore carries a different standard deviation from the gross active return series.
rationales.B: Performance-based fee structures may lead to misestimates of portfolio risk. Such fee structures convert symmetrical gross active return distributions into asymmetrical net active return distributions, reducing variability on the upside but not on the downside. As a result, a single standard deviation calculated on a return series that incorporates active returns above and below the base fee can lead to the underestimation of downside risk. A management fee lowers the level of realized return without affecting the standard deviation, whereas a performance fee has the added effect of lowering the realized standard deviation.
rationales.C: The distortion runs in the opposite direction. By truncating variability on the upside while leaving the downside intact, these structures make a single standard deviation computed on net active returns understate the downside, so downside risk is underestimated rather than overstated.

drills.los_text: analyze and interpret a sample performance-based fee schedule

questions.stem: A simple performance-based fee schedule is symmetrical around a standard fee of 0.50%, has a breakeven active return of 1.50%, and gives the manager no share of active performance beyond 2.75%. The schedule's remaining parameters are most likely:

options.A: Base fee 0.25%, 50% sharing, no fee cap.
options.B: Base fee 0.25%, 20% sharing, 0.75% fee cap.
options.C: Base fee 0.50%, 20% sharing, 0.75% fee cap.

rationales.A: A 50% sharing rate with no cap does not fit the schedule. Sharing applies to active return beyond the base fee, so with a 0.25% base fee and 50% sharing the computed fee at 1.50% active return would be 0.25% + 0.50 x (1.50% - 0.25%) = 0.875%, not the 0.50% standard fee; the breakeven active return would instead be 0.75%. An uncapped structure also contradicts the absence of sharing beyond 2.75% active return, which is precisely what produces a maximum annual fee.
rationales.B: The standard fee is 0.50% and the base fee is 0.25%. The base fee is a floor below which the computed fee can never fall, so the manager is protected against sharing for performance below 25 bps. Sharing is 20% of active return beyond the base fee, which makes the breakeven active return 1.50%: 0.25% + 0.20 x (1.50% - 0.25%) = 0.50%, equal to the standard fee. To make the result symmetrical around the commonplace 50 bps fee, the manager does not share in active performance beyond 2.75%, which caps the maximum annual fee at 0.25% + 0.20 x (2.75% - 0.25%) = 0.75%, as far above the 0.50% standard fee as the 0.25% base fee is below it.
rationales.C: This swaps the two fees. The standard fee is 0.50% and the base fee, the floor below which the computed fee cannot fall, is 0.25%. A 0.50% base fee would make the computed fee at least equal to the standard fee at all times, so the breakeven active return would be 0.50% rather than 1.50%, and ending sharing at 2.75% would cap the fee at 0.50% + 0.20 x (2.75% - 0.50%) = 0.95% rather than 0.75%.

questions.stem: A performance-based fee schedule bills a 0.25% base fee plus 20% of active return beyond the base fee, subject to a maximum annual fee of 0.75%. For an annual period, the pairing of billed fee and net active return that is most likely correct is:

options.A: Active return 1.50%: fee 0.75%, net 0.75%.
options.B: Active return 0.25%: fee 0.00%, net 0.25%.
options.C: Active return 0.25%: fee 0.25%, net 0.00%.

rationales.A: At 1.50% active return the billed fee is 0.25% + 0.20 x (1.50% - 0.25%) = 0.50%, leaving a net active return of 1.00%, not a 0.75% fee and 0.75% net. The 0.75% maximum annual fee is not reached until active return of 2.75% or more, where the billed fee is 0.25% + 0.20 x (2.75% - 0.25%) = 0.75% and the net active return is 2.00% or more.
rationales.B: The 0.25% base fee is a floor that is billed even when there is no active return to share, so at active return of 0.25% or less the billed fee is 0.25%, not 0.00%. Net active return is therefore 0.00% or less rather than positive.
rationales.C: At active return of 0.25% or less the billed fee is the 0.25% base fee and net active return is 0.00% or less. The full schedule for annual periods runs: active return 0.25% or less, billed fee 0.25%, net active return 0.00% or less; 1.00%, 0.40%, 0.60%; 1.50%, 0.50%, 1.00%; 2.00%, 0.60%, 1.40%; 2.75% or more, 0.75%, 2.00% or more. Each billed fee is the base fee plus 20% of active return beyond the base fee, so at 1.00% active return the fee is 0.25% + 0.20 x (1.00% - 0.25%) = 0.40%, and at 2.00% it is 0.25% + 0.20 x 1.75% = 0.60%, until the 0.75% maximum annual fee binds at 2.75%.

questions.stem: Performance-based fees paid to a manager on active return are most likely best described as:

options.A: extra manager compensation with no economic function.
options.B: full removal of the investor's exposure to manager luck.
options.C: risk sharing between the investor and the manager.

rationales.A: Performance-based fees do have an economic function. If investment outcomes result from a mix of skill and luck, that is, a probability distribution around a positive mean alpha, then performance fees constitute risk sharing rather than merely additional compensation. They work to align the interests of managers and investors because both parties share in investment results, and investors benefit by paying performance-based fees rather than standard fees when active returns are low.
rationales.B: The sharing is partial, not complete. The investor still bears outcome variability; the fee structure reallocates part of it rather than eliminating the investor's exposure to the luck component of the outcome. This is why fee structures must be designed carefully to avoid favoring one party over the other.
rationales.C: If investment outcomes result from a mix of skill and luck, that is, a probability distribution around a positive mean alpha, then performance fees constitute risk sharing. Fee structures must be designed carefully to avoid favoring one party over the other. Performance-based fees work to align the interests of managers and investors because both parties share in investment results. Investors benefit by paying performance-based fees, rather than standard fees, when active returns are low, and managers may work harder to earn performance-based fees, which inspires the alternative term incentive based.

questions.stem: Empirical evidence on performance-based fees most likely associates them with:

options.A: no difference in realized performance.
options.B: lower alphas, from excessive risk taking.
options.C: higher alphas and higher risk-adjusted returns.

rationales.A: The evidence does show a relationship between fee structure and results. Performance-based fees are correlated with higher alphas, and also with lower fees, for mutual funds, and with higher risk-adjusted returns for hedge funds (Elton, Gruber, and Blake 2003; Ackermann, McEnally, and Ravenscraft 1999).
rationales.B: The documented correlation runs positive for alpha, not negative. Performance-based fees are associated with higher alphas, and with lower total fees, for mutual funds, and with higher risk-adjusted returns for hedge funds, rather than with alpha destroyed by excessive risk taking.
rationales.C: Empirical evidence suggests a correlation between performance-based fees and higher alphas, and also lower fees, for mutual funds, and higher risk-adjusted returns for hedge funds (Elton, Gruber, and Blake 2003; Ackermann, McEnally, and Ravenscraft 1999). Asset managers may consider performance-based fees attractive because such fees provide an opportunity to enhance profits on the upside and ensure guaranteed, although perhaps minimal, streams of revenue from base fees when performance is poor.

questions.stem: Under a performance-based fee structure, it is most likely that:

options.A: investors pay base fees even when managers underperform.
options.B: base fees are waived when managers underperform.
options.C: poor-performing managers fail less often than under standard fees.

rationales.A: Performance-based fees can create tensions between investors and managers. Investors must pay base fees even when managers underperform. At the same time, management firm revenues decline when cash is needed to invest in operations or retain talent. In fact, the failure rate for poor-performing and even zero-alpha managers may tend to be higher when performance-based rather than standard fees are used.
rationales.B: Base fees are not waived. Investors must pay base fees even when managers underperform, and that obligation is itself one of the tensions a performance-based fee structure creates between investor and manager.
rationales.C: The failure rate for poor-performing and even zero-alpha managers may tend to be higher, not lower, when performance-based rather than standard fees are used, because management firm revenues decline at exactly the point when cash is needed to invest in operations or retain talent.

questions.stem: Regarding option-like bonus fees and a manager's risk taking, the most likely statement is that:

options.A: bonus fees give no incentive to alter portfolio risk.
options.B: compensation should reward risk taking without penalty.
options.C: higher volatility raises the bonus fee's value, encouraging more risk.

rationales.A: A bonus fee is option-like, and based on option pricing theory higher volatility leads to higher option value, which encourages managers to assume higher portfolio risk. This behavior has been observed in the marketplace. The offsetting pressures are not the absence of an incentive but the need to retain clients year to year, to avoid poor performance, and not to violate management guidelines.
rationales.B: Senior management at investment firms should ensure that compensation systems penalize portfolio managers for assuming excessive risk as well as reward them for earning superior returns. Rewarding risk taking without penalty would reinforce the incentive the option-like fee already creates, since higher volatility raises the value of the manager's option rather than benefiting the investor.
rationales.C: Managers must retain clients year to year, avoid poor performance, and not violate management guidelines, but managers also tend to have an interest in increasing risk, which may conflict with these goals. Based on option pricing theory, higher volatility leads to higher option value, which encourages managers to assume higher portfolio risk, and this behavior has been observed in the marketplace. As a result, investors, when possible, should carefully select benchmarks and monitor risk in their portfolios, and senior management at investment firms should also ensure that their compensation systems penalize portfolio managers for assuming excessive risk as well as reward them for earning superior returns.

questions.stem: In assessing manager skill and designing manager compensation, it is most likely that:

options.A: gross excess return suffices to show the investor benefits.
options.B: more convex, option-like compensation is preferred.
options.C: more linear compensation is preferred.

rationales.A: The presence of a positive, significant average excess return is evidence for manager skill, but that excess return must be net of fees and expenses for the benefit of the skill to accrue to the investor. A gross figure can be consumed entirely by fees and expenses, leaving the investor no better off.
rationales.B: The stated preference runs the other way. More linear compensation is preferred because convex, option-like payoffs give the manager an incentive to change the portfolio's risk profile at the inflection points where the fee schedule bends.
rationales.C: The presence of positive significant average excess return is evidence for manager skill. This excess return, however, must be net of fees and expenses for the benefit of this skill to accrue to the investor. The preference is for more linear compensation to the manager, in order to reduce the incentives to change the portfolio's risk profile at inflection points.
